title: The Year of the Elephant
subtitle: Before his birth, the world already bowed to his coming
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the opening of the biography
Qur'an 105 (Surah Al-Fil) — the armies of the elephant

chapters.heading: Abraha's Army and the Falling Birds
chapters.body: In the year the Prophet ﷺ was born, Abraha al-Ashram, the Christian ruler of Yemen, built a magnificent cathedral in Sana'a — and then marched on Makkah with elephants to pull the Arabs away from the Kaaba to his new shrine. The Qur'an compressed that arrogance into five verses: 'Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? Did He not make their plot go astray, and send against them birds in flocks, striking them with stones of hard clay, and He made them like eaten straw?' (105:1-5). The seerah of Ibn Ishaq records what the Arabs called that year forever after: the Year of the Elephant — the year the Kabah humbled an empire, months before the boy was born who would make that humble House the qiblah of the world. From his first breath, history arranged itself around him.

familyQuestion: Allah defended His House with birds. What big threat in your life might look smaller if you remembered Who is defending you?

title: The Orphan of Makkah
subtitle: Amina's son, Halimah's milk, Abu Talib's shadow
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the fosterage and the opening years
Sahih al-Bukhari 5101 — Halimah's account of the blessed fosterage

chapters.heading: The Child Who Brought Blessing
chapters.body: Muhammad ﷺ was born in the Year of the Elephant, son of Abdullah ibn Abdul-Muttalib and Amina bint Wahb. His father died before his birth, and by desert custom he was given to a foster mother of Banu Sa'd — and the seerah records that Halimah's household, poor and dry, blossomed the moment she took him: her flock fattened, her milk flowed, and she pressed to keep the child an extra season (Sahih al-Bukhari 5101). At six, his mother Amina died on the road home from Madinah at a place called Abwa, and the boy came back to Makkah an orphan twice over. His grandfather Abdul-Muttalib took him in and adored him — keeping the child beside him in the council of Quraysh where no child had ever sat — and when the old man died, Muhammad ﷺ passed to his uncle Abu Talib, who guarded him for forty years. The Qur'an would one day name his condition over him: 'Did He not find you an orphan and shelter you?' (93:6). Orphanhood was his first teacher; protection was his Lord's first gift.

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ lost his parents as a small child and was still raised with love. Who shelters the vulnerable people around you — and could that be you?

title: Al-Amin, The Trustworthy
subtitle: The honest young man the Quraysh could not bribe
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the merchant of Khadijah and the rebuilding of the Kaaba
Sahih al-Bukhari 3820 — Khadijah's testimony to his character

chapters.heading: The Merchant of Makkah
chapters.body: As a young man, Muhammad ﷺ entered the caravan trade, and the seerah records that the merchants learned to trust him above their own accountants — so much that the wealthy Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, hearing of his honesty, sent him her capital to trade in Syria with her servant Maysarah. The journey returned double its profit and Maysarah returned with a story: two angels had shaded him from the sun. Khadijah proposed marriage through a friend, and though she was fifteen years his senior and the nobles of Makkah had sought her, she chose the orphan of Abu Talib. Years later, when revelation first shook him, her answer named the character of his whole youth: 'You keep good relations with your kin, you help the weak, you honor the guest, you bear the hardship of the road, you help against the calamities of truth' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3). Makkah's nickname for him before any revelation was simple: Al-Amin — the Trustworthy.

familyQuestion: Khadijah listed five habits that proved his prophethood. Which of the five — kin, the weak, guests, hardship, truth — needs your work this month?

title: The Cave of Hira
subtitle: Forty years of silence before the first word
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the retreat to Hira
Sahih al-Bukhari 3-4 — the narration of Aisha on the first revelation

chapters.heading: Solitude Before the Storm
chapters.body: In his late thirties, Muhammad ﷺ began leaving Makkah's noise for the cave of Hira on Jabal an-Nur, taking provisions and turning his face to the silence. The seerah records that he would stay days at a time in the cave, thinking — a man of Makkah withdrawing from Makkah, troubled by the idols he had never bowed to. In the month of Ramadan, in the year he turned forty, the silence ended. The angel came to him and said: Iqra — Read. He answered: I am not one who can read. The angel embraced him until it was more than he could bear, then released him and repeated the command — three times — until the words descended: 'Read in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clot. Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know' (96:1-5). The first word of the final revelation was not a command to rule or to fight. It was a command to read, in the name of the One who created — and the first description of the Lord it gave was not power, but generosity (96:3).

chapters.heading: Khadijah's Test
chapters.body: He ran home from the cave trembling, asking to be covered, and told Khadijah what he had seen — and her response, preserved in Bukhari's Sahih, became the first theology of the new religion: 'Never! By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You keep good relations with your kin, you help the weak, you honor the guest, you bear the hardship of the road, you help against the calamities of truth' (Bukhari 3). Notice: the first believer reasoned from character to truth. Then she took him to her cousin Waraqa ibn Nawfal, a Christian scholar, who heard the description and said the words that confirmed everything: 'This is the same one who keeps the secrets whom Allah had sent to Moses' (Bukhari 3). The first consultant of the prophethood was a woman; the first confirmation came from a Christian scholar who knew the scriptures. From its first hour, this message crossed every boundary people build.

familyQuestion: The first command of the final revelation was Iqra — Read. What is your relationship with reading — and could one good book change your family's next year?

title: Three Years of Whispers
subtitle: The secret call — the low classes of Makkah believe first
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the private preaching
Musnad Ahmad 15493 — Ali's account of the feast

chapters.heading: The Feast of Abdul-Muttalib
chapters.body: For three years the call moved quietly — from house to house, trusted friend to trusted friend. Khadijah believed first, then Ali the boy in his household, then Zayd his freedman — and in that order, the seerah scholars note, was the whole future of the ummah prefigured: a woman, a youth, a freed slave. When the command came — 'And warn your nearest kindred' (26:214) — Muhammad ﷺ climbed Safa and called the clans of Quraysh, asking them: if I told you horsemen were in this valley, would you believe me? They said: yes, we have never found you but truthful. He said: then I am a warner before a severe punishment (Bukhari 3527). Abu Lahab cursed him and left — and a verse descended on that day naming the uncle's end (111:1-5). Then he gathered Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib for a meal, the feast of which Ali's narration survives (Ahmad 15493): 'Which of you will assist me in this matter, so that he is my brother, my executor, my successor among you?' The room fell silent — and Ali, barely into his teens, stood and said: I will, though I am the youngest. Muhammad ﷺ placed his hand on Ali's neck and said: this is my brother, my successor among you.

familyQuestion: The first believers were a woman, a teenager, and a freed slave. What does that tell you about whose hearts Allah chooses first?

title: Bilal and the Heavy Sand
subtitle: The slave who taught the world a word: Ahad
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the persecution of the weak believers
Sunan al-Tirmidhi 3754 — Abu Bakr's freeing of Bilal

chapters.heading: Ahad, Ahad
chapters.body: When the call went public and Quraysh could not bribe or debate it down, they turned to the believers who had no tribe to shield them. Bilal ibn Rabah, the Abyssinian slave, was dragged at noon onto the burning sand of Makkah, a boulder pressed on his chest, and told to renounce — and his answer, seared into every generation since, was one word: Ahad — One. One God. Umayyah ibn Khalaf tortured him past the limits of endurance, and it was Abu Bakr who passed by and said the sentence that purchased a civilization: 'Are you not content that he says Allah is my Lord and you have his blood on your hands?... By Allah, if you kill him in this way I will make his example the most remembered example in Makkah' (Tirmidhi 3754). Abu Bakr exchanged Bilal for a non-Muslim slave of greater strength — and freed him. The men with nothing became the carriers of everything: Bilal, Ammar, Sumayyah, Suhayb, Khabbab — the weak of Makkah out-argued its chiefs and out-suffered its torturers, and the truth did not need the strong to survive. It needed the sincere.

familyQuestion: Bilal had one word under a boulder: Ahad. If your faith cost you comfort today, what would your one word be?

title: The Night of the Journey
subtitle: Al-Isra wal-Mi'raj — five prayers as the gift of the heavens
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 349 — the full narration of the Night Journey
Qur'an 17:1 — 'Exalted is He who took His servant by night'
Sahih Muslim 162 — the fifty prayers reduced to five

chapters.heading: From the Haram to the Farthest Mosque
chapters.body: In the year of Abu Talib's death — the Year of Sorrow — the Prophet ﷺ was carried from the sacred mosque to the farthest mosque in a single night: 'Exalted is He who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed' (17:1). From Jerusalem he ascended through the heavens — Bukhari preserves the narration in full — past Adam at the first heaven, Isa and Yahya, Yusuf, Idris, Harun, Musa, and Ibrahim leaning against the Bayt al-Ma'mur, to where 'there was no veil between him and his Lord' except what the eye of his heart could bear. Musa asked him at the end what his nation had been given, and when he heard fifty prayers a day, Musa said: your people cannot bear fifty — go back and ask your Lord to lighten it (Bukhari 349, Muslim 162). He returned and returned again, until the covenant stood at five prayers for the reward of fifty — 'the word of your Lord will be fulfilled: there is no changing My words' — and Muhammad ﷺ said: I returned to my Lord until He said these are five, and they are fifty; the word is not changed (Muslim 162). The five daily prayers are not a burden negotiated down. They are a gift negotiated up — from the Lord of the heavens, through the stubborn love of Musa for the believers, to your doorstep five times a day.

familyQuestion: Five prayers were gifted from above the seven heavens. Do you treat them as a burden negotiated down — or a gift you get to keep?

title: The Boycott
subtitle: Three years in the valley — the written siege
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the document of the boycott
Qur'an 111 — 'May the hands of Abu Lahab perish'

chapters.heading: A Document Against a Clan
chapters.body: When persuasion, bribery, and torture failed, Quraysh tried isolation. The clans wrote a document — the seerah records its hanging inside the Kaaba — binding themselves: no marrying the Banu Hashim, no selling to them, no sitting with them, until they surrendered Muhammad ﷺ to be killed. The document turned Makkah into a prison for one clan. For three years the Hashim and al-Muttalib, Muslims and non-Muslims among them alike, ate leaves and the milk of a single she-camel, in the stony valley outside the city. Khadijah's wealth drained away in those years — the seerah historians count the boycott among the causes of her death soon after. And then the tide turned from an unexpected place: some Qurayshis themselves, sickened by watching relatives starve, began passing food secretly; then Hisham ibn Amr and others worked openly until the document — which, the tradition records, termites had devoured except the words 'in Your name, O Allah' — was declared void by the very men who wrote it. A starving clan had outlasted an empire's merchant aristocracy, and the famine broke before the faith did.

familyQuestion: The boycott starved the Muslims for three years but broke before their faith did. What pressure are you under that only feels permanent?
